<reason>Side A wins by showing the ban is overbroad: concentrated local harm supports well-specific caps, drought suspensions, fees, and monitoring, not prohibition of sustainable extraction. A also answers the takings pressure with a credible prospective-versus-retroactive distinction and exposes the cost and capacity problems in B's publicly funded replacement. B's capture, export, and public-infrastructure arguments remain forceful, but do not establish that workable regulation must fail everywhere.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>The decisive exchange was B's takings contradiction challenge, blunted by A's A4.1 distinction between enforcing conditions accepted in new or renewed permits and retroactively extinguishing existing rights through a categorical ban.</best_rebuttal>
